qs.q: A patient with chronic renal failure presents with persistently low serum calcium and elevated serum phosphate levels. What is the expected compensatory response by the parathyroid glands?
o: Parathyroid gland atrophy with decreased PTH
qs.e: Secondary hyperparathyroidism occurs in renal failure as a compensatory mechanism to maintain calcium homeostasis in response to phosphate retention and low active vitamin D. Autonomous PTH overproduction defines primary hyperparathyroidism.

qs.q: A 10-year-old child presents with chronic renal failure, haematuria, partial lipodystrophy, and retinal drusen. Serology confirms markedly low serum C3. What specific immunohistochemical finding distinguishes this patient's glomerular disease from MPGN Type I?
o: Presence of C3 staining alone without IgG, C1q, or C4
Granular subendothelial deposits of IgG along capillary loops
Positive staining for polyclonal IgG4 and kappa light chains
Dense linear staining of the glomerular basement membrane
qs.e: Dense deposit disease features C3 staining alone on immunofluorescence without IgG, C1q, or C4, which clearly distinguishes it from MPGN Type I where immune complexes yield IgG and C1q deposition. The presence of C3 alone reflects alternative pathway dysregulation rather than classical immune complex deposition.

qs.q: A 35-year-old male with chronic renal failure presents with severe lethargy and pallor. Laboratory results show a low red blood cell count. Which specific growth factor is primarily deficient in this patient?
qs.e: Erythropoietin (EPO) is of renal origin and triggers red blood cell production in response to hypoxia. Thrombopoietin regulates platelets, while G-CSF/GM-CSF drive granulocytes.

qs.q: A patient with chronic renal failure develops metabolic acidosis with an increased anion gap. At approximately what GFR level does this uremic acidosis typically develop?
o: A measured GFR level below 120 mL/min
A measured GFR level below 80 mL/min
A measured GFR level below 50 mL/min
A measured GFR level below 20 mL/min
qs.e: Uremic acidosis develops when the GFR falls below 20 mL/min (with creatinine greater than 350 micromol/L) due to decreased hydrogen ion excretion. Higher GFR thresholds are seen in earlier stages of renal functional decline without overt uremic acidosis.

qs.q: Fluid overload in chronic renal failure typically results from the failure of sodium and free water excretion when the GFR drops below what level?
qs.e: Fluid overload results from the failure of sodium and free water excretion usually at a GFR below 10-15 mL/min. Patients present with peripheral and often pulmonary edema along with hypertension.

qs.q: Hypocalcemia develops in chronic renal failure primarily due to which of the following factors?
o: Decreased intestinal calcium absorption from low plasma calcitriol
Direct urinary wasting of ionized calcium via damaged tubules
Excessive calcitonin release from the surrounding thyroid gland
Suppression of parathyroid hormone synthesis by uremic toxins
qs.e: Hypocalcemia develops primarily from decreased intestinal calcium absorption because of low plasma calcitriol levels and possibly from calcium binding to elevated serum levels of phosphate. This low calcium further triggers PTH synthesis and secretion.

qs.q: In secondary hyperparathyroidism due to chronic renal failure, PTH levels are usually
qs.e: Chronic renal failure leads to phosphate retention and impaired vitamin D activation, causing hypocalcemia. This chronically stimulates the parathyroid glands, leading to compensatory hyperplasia and markedly elevated PTH levels.

qs.q: A patient with chronic renal failure develops hyperphosphatemia. This is because the failing kidneys are unable to
qs.e: Healthy kidneys filter and excrete phosphate. In chronic renal failure, this filtration capacity is reduced, leading to phosphate retention (hyperphosphatemia). This also contributes to hypocalcemia, which stimulates PTH secretion.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Chronic renal failure is the gradual loss of kidney function over months to years, driven mainly by diabetes, hypertension, or glomerulonephritis. It presents with fatigue, edema, and metabolic derangements that worsen as GFR falls.

sections.p: Chronic renal failure (CRF) is defined by a GFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m² for ≥3 months or markers of kidney damage such as albuminuria. Diagnosis relies on eGFR, urine albumin, and imaging to rule out obstruction.

t.b: Low eGFR indicates reduced filtration; the lower the value, the more advanced the disease.
Elevated ratio shows glomerular leakage, a hallmark of CKD.
Normal size kidneys with no obstruction support a functional decline rather than an anatomical block.

sections.p: CKD is staged 1–5 by eGFR and albuminuria. Stage 5 (end‑stage) requires dialysis or transplant. Staging guides treatment intensity and monitoring frequency.
b: Stage 1: eGFR ≥90 mL/min/1.73 m², albuminuria present
Stage 5: eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73 m², dialysis indicated

t.b: It determines prognosis and treatment thresholds.

sections.p: The leading causes are diabetic nephropathy, hypertensive nephrosclerosis, and glomerulonephritis. In low‑resource settings, infections (HIV, TB, malaria), herbal nephrotoxins, and sickle cell disease also contribute.

t.b: High HbA1c predicts progression of diabetic nephropathy.
Persistently high BP accelerates nephron loss.

sections.p: Early CKD is often silent. As it progresses, patients develop fatigue, anorexia, edema, hypertension, and uremic symptoms such as nausea and pruritus. Children may show growth retardation.

t.b: Hypertension is both a cause and consequence of CKD.
High potassium can cause cardiac arrhythmias.

sections.p: Key tests assess kidney function, damage, and complications. When resources are limited, focus on creatinine, urinalysis, and basic electrolytes.

t.b: Proteinuria signals glomerular injury; hematuria suggests glomerulonephritis or obstruction.
Hyperkalemia risks arrhythmia; hyperphosphatemia causes bone disease.
Low bicarbonate reflects loss of acid excretion.
Normal size with no obstruction supports functional decline.

sections.p: Rapid decline in eGFR, uncontrolled hypertension, hyperkalemia, severe anemia, or signs of volume overload warrant urgent care. Complications include cardiovascular disease, bone disease, and electrolyte imbalance.

t.b: Such levels risk stroke or heart failure.

faq.q: What is the most common cause of CKD worldwide?
faq.a: Diabetes mellitus is the leading cause, followed by hypertension.
Early stages may be slowed or stabilized with treatment, but irreversible loss of nephrons cannot be reversed.
Reduced erythropoietin production by damaged kidneys lowers red cell production.
